title: We're Getting Death Threats for Resisting EdTech
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin, known as The Screentime Consultant and lead plaintiff in a class action against a major EdTech company, publishes her full statement to a September 15, 2026 NTIA listening session feeding into an FCC proceeding on the E-Rate program, which funds school connectivity. Her core claim is that EdTech is Big Tech in a sweater vest: the harms attributed to social platforms, including problematic content, excessive use and degraded focus, empathy and critical thinking, are also occurring on the 1:1 devices used by over 90 percent of American schoolchildren. She illustrates this with a cascade of classroom examples, from second graders reading on iPads with no books on their desks to gambling ads during typing lessons. Cherkin sets out four conditions any classroom technology should meet before reaching children: it must be effective, safe, legal and superior to a human teacher. She describes growing momentum for opt-out policies and AI bans, alongside a backlash that has included hate mail calling for activists to be assassinated. Rejecting the Luddite label, she describes her position as tech-intentional, and closes by urging regulators not to let E-Rate become a subsidy for bandwidth-hungry EdTech products whose business model is engagement rather than learning.
points: Cherkin argues that school-issued devices reproduce the same harms as consumer social media, so EdTech should be regulated and scrutinised as Big Tech.
She proposes a four-part test before any tech product reaches children: effective, safe, legal, and superior to a human teacher.
Parents who restrict screens at home discover school devices open to apps, sites, data collection and chatbots, which she says makes it hard to call this a parenting problem.
The movement against classroom EdTech has won opt-out policies and AI bans but also provoked a backlash, including a death threat she quotes from her hate mail.
On policy, she argues E-Rate is being used to fund premium broadband that EdTech products require, effectively subsidising engagement-driven companies rather than basic school connectivity.
quotes: The same harms, problematic content, excessive use, and degradation of focus, empathy, and critical thinking skills that we hear about occurring on platforms like Snapchat and Meta are occurring on the internet-connected 1:1 devices and EdTech products used by over 90% of American schoolchildren.
These students are engaged in “reading.” There are no books on their desks. Instead, they are wearing headphones and plugged into iPads, on which they swipe digital “pages” to advance the “book.

Recently, an IT professional with 20 years of experience, whose role is to set up computers for corporate professionals, told me she was absolutely appalled by what she saw in the Chromebook that came home with her child– a lack of regulation and oversight that would never be permitted in a corporate workplace.

And families who have restricted their children’s use of screens before entering school are horrified to learn the iPad the school sent home has access to apps and websites they never would have approved. It’s hard to argue this is a “parenting” problem when these devices are provided by the school.

Just like we test the brakes on a car before we send it to the dealership; just like we perform trials before giving medication to the wider population; we must ask whether these products are safe, legal, effective, and better than the teacher they are clearly intended to replace.

My colleagues and I are not opposed to technology. We support computer labs with trained instructors, technology education programs (vs. EdTech products), and even the occasional use of digital tools that offer something an analog approach cannot.

EdTech products do not function without the internet, and to operate fully, they require significantly more broadband than what’s needed for a simple internet search, email, or typing class. Programs like eRate are being taken advantage of to benefit companies whose products won’t run on anything but “premium” levels of broadband, when a lower level would suffice for teacher and staff needs.
